generatedCommentsNodes.comment: The `timeStampSpec` instance is shared across `TIME_SERIES_SORT`, `TIMESTAMP_SORT`, and `HOSTNAME_TIMESTAMP_SORT`. This is currently safe because the code paths that use these arrays always return before reaching the mutation loops (`sortSpecs[i].order = ...`). However, this is a latent maintenance hazard: if a future change removes an early return or adds a new code path that mutates sort specs, it would silently corrupt the other shared arrays. Consider creating independent `FieldSortSpec` instances for each array to eliminate the shared-mutable-state risk.

In `getMappingData`, when `LOGSDB_SORT_ON_HOST_NAME` is explicitly `false` in the request settings but the mapping contains a `host.name` field mapper, the returned `MappingData` has `sortOnHostName = true` (because of the `||` with the `instanceof FieldMapper` check). Then in `getAdditionalIndexSettings`, the provider injects `index.logsdb.use_default_sort_config=true`, silently overriding the user's explicit `false`. Consider whether the user's explicit `false` should be respected (i.e., short-circuit to `sortOnHostName = false` when the setting is explicitly present and `false`), or document that this setting is purely internal and should not be set by users.

The refactoring moves the `DiscoveryNode.isStateless` check from a guard around `init()` to a parameter. This means `mapperServiceFactory` is now always set (even for stateless), so `getMappingData` will actually create a `MapperService` for stateless deployments when it reaches the mapper-service code path. Previously, for stateless, `mapperServiceFactory.get()` would throw (SetOnce not set) and the catch block would return `MappingData.EMPTY`. Verify that creating a `MapperService` in stateless mode is safe and doesn't have side effects (e.g., file system access, resource leaks) that were previously avoided.

The test asserts `hasPrimarySortOnField("host.name")` equals `sortOnHostName`, but this only holds when the index version is `>= LOGSB_OPTIONAL_SORTING_ON_HOST_NAME`. The test relies on `IndexSettingsTests.newIndexMeta` setting a sufficiently recent version. If that helper ever defaults to an older version, the BWC path would always return `true` and the test would fail for `sortOnHostName = false`. Consider explicitly setting the index version in the test metadata to make the intent clear and guard against regressions.

The error messages in the LOGSDB no-explicit-sort-fields branch are misleading. When `INDEX_SORT_ORDER_SETTING` (or mode/missing) is present without `INDEX_SORT_FIELD_SETTING`, the thrown message says "size mismatch" and includes `fields` which is an empty list at that point (e.g., `"index.sort.fields:[] index.sort.order:[desc], size mismatch"`). The actual problem is that these companion settings are not allowed without an explicit `index.sort.field` — it's not a size mismatch. A clearer message would be something like:
```java
throw new IllegalArgumentException(
    "index.sort.order cannot be set without index.sort.field for logsdb indices"
);
```
The same applies to the `index.sort.mode` and `index.sort.missing` checks immediately below.

review_comment:
Just to verify my understanding of why we need this setting. Is it for cases where the mapping does contain a `host.name` field but the user doesn't want it to be used for sorting purposes? I suppose that is to have parity with the previous behavior where you could disable sorting by `host.name` by manually specifying just `@timestamp` as a sort field. Did I get that right?

Nit: there's a discrepancy in the naming (`SORT_ON_HOST_NAME` vs `use_default_sort_config`). The latter seems a bit more generic in case we add more fields to the default sort config. But either way, I think it makes sense to keep the name of the config option and the constant aligned.

The idea here is that, if we detect that the mappings contain a field (not object) `host.name`, it's used for sorting. Otherwise, we only sort on `@timestamp`. The rationale is that there's no point to inject `host.name` and sort on it if the mappings don't indicate that it's already present and used.

Good catch about the discrepancy - initially I had 2 settings to separately control injecting `host.name` and sorting on it. It feels cleaner to skip injection, but I'm really interested on your take here.

As mentioned in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/118968#discussion_r1899523137, I think it's important to still support dynamically mapped `host.name` fields. This could either be achieved by injecting `host.name` or by introducing this sorting hash we talked about.
Wouldn't `host.name` get injected from a dynamic template in this case? What if `host` gets dynamically mapped to a keyword as well, without `subobjects:false`?

> Wouldn't host.name get injected from a dynamic template in this case?

Not entirely sure what you mean. But there doesn't need to be a dynamic template that's specific to `host.name`, it could just be one that maps strings to keywords by default.

> What if host gets dynamically mapped to a keyword as well, without subobjects:false?

That would be an issue indeed. Still better than the current default that always injects the host.name. I suppose we'll eventually need a solution that doesn't depend on injecting a mapping but also fully supports dynamic mappings. The only solution that comes to my mind that reconciles the two is the sorting hash approach.
ok I've restored the second setting for injecting `host.name` when possible.
